Throttle has three distinct but deeply connected layers of meaning. Once you understand all three, you'll never be confused by this word again — no matter where you encounter it.
The Core, Literal Meaning: To Choke or Strangle

At its most direct, to throttle someone means to grip their throat tightly and squeeze — cutting off their airway or blood flow. It's a violent, deliberate act of choking with your hands.

The attacker throttled his victim until she went limp.

This is the root image the word carries. It's more intense than accidental choking — throttling implies someone is forcefully and intentionally gripping a throat to suppress the flow of life itself. Hold that image in your mind, because it's the heart of everything this word means.

The Figurative Meaning: To Suppress or Strangle Something into Submission

Because throttling physically cuts off something vital, the word extends naturally to situations where something — not a person's throat, but an idea, a freedom, a business, a voice — is being suppressed so severely that it can barely survive or function.

The authoritarian government throttled the free press.
Heavy taxes throttled economic growth.
His overbearing management style throttled his team's creativity.

Notice the word does more work than simply saying "limit" or "reduce." When you throttle something figuratively, you're suggesting a suffocating, iron-grip kind of restriction — something is being held down so tightly it's gasping. It conveys force and severity. A minor inconvenience doesn't throttle something; a crushing, stifling force does.
The Technical Meaning: To Regulate or Control a Rate of Flow

This is where the word shifts from violent to neutral — even clinical. In engineering and technology, to throttle something means to deliberately restrict or control the rate at which something flows or operates, in order to regulate it precisely.

The word is used in two common technical areas:

In engines, throttling means controlling the flow of fuel and air into the engine, which directly controls its power and speed. When a pilot or driver "throttles back," they're reducing that flow to slow down or reduce power. The accelerator in a car is literally called a throttle because it performs this function.

The pilot throttled back the engines as the aircraft descended.

In internet and computing, when a service provider "throttles" your connection, they deliberately slow down your data speed — restricting how much data can flow to you per second, usually after you've hit a usage limit.

My streaming was choppy because my carrier was throttling my data.
The server throttles incoming requests to prevent itself from being overwhelmed.

Here, throttling isn't necessarily cruel — it's a controlled, calculated restriction of flow to manage a system's capacity.
The Single Thread Running Through All Three Meanings

Whether the word is used literally (strangling a person), figuratively (crushing a business or a freedom), or technically (capping data speed or engine power) — the core idea is always the same: a forceful constriction that controls, limits, or cuts off the flow of something. The severity ranges from deadly violence to precise mechanical regulation, but every usage shares that central image of a tight grip on something, controlling how much it gets to breathe, flow, or function.

These phrases mean to deliberately pull back, slow down, or reduce the intensity of something. They come from the engine sense but are freely used in everyday figurative language.

After a frantic first quarter, the startup decided to throttle back its hiring.
The new manager asked the team to throttle down the pace and focus on quality.

Both mean: ease off — reduce how hard or fast something is running.
A Quick Summary of All the Senses

To throttle can mean to physically strangle someone by the throat; to suppress or stifle something (a freedom, a business, creativity) so forcefully that it can barely survive; or to regulate and restrict the rate of a flow (fuel, data, engine power) in a controlled way. To throttle back or throttle down means to deliberately reduce speed, power, or intensity.
